description: Buying or selling in Surprise, AZ? Teigh Wade, REALTOR®, lives here. Learn the communities, home types, HOAs, freeways and what to check before you move.
summary: Surprise is an incorporated city in Maricopa County's northwest Valley, reached by Loop 303 and US-60 (Grand Avenue). Most homes sit in master-planned communities such as Sun City Grand, Marley Park and Surprise Farms, so HOAs are common. Teigh Wade, REALTOR®, lives in Surprise and helps buyers and sellers here.

sections.html:
Surprise is where Teigh Wade lives, so this is the part of the Valley she knows street by street. The city sits in the northwest corner of the Phoenix area in Maricopa County. It was founded in 1938 by Flora Mae Statler and incorporated as a city in 1960. The first lots were laid out as modest housing for farm workers, and the city has grown outward from that original townsite ever since.

Today Surprise is a sprawling city of subdivisions, golf courses, shopping corridors and open desert pushing toward the White Tank Mountains. Bell Road is the main east-west commercial spine. The Surprise Recreation Campus near Bell Road and Bullard Avenue holds Surprise Stadium, the spring training home of the Texas Rangers and the Kansas City Royals, along with Surprise Community Park, a fishing lake, tennis and pickleball courts, and dog parks. The Oasis Swim center opened on the campus in 2025.

A few local details make Surprise feel like its own place. City Hall stands on the site of a former Luke Air Force Base auxiliary airfield, and the old runways still show up in aerial photos. The Southwest Railplex industrial park and Foreign Trade Zone sits in the southeast corner of the city.

Most of the housing stock in Surprise was built from the mid-1990s onward, and a good share went up in the 2000s building boom. Expect stucco exteriors, tile or concrete roofs, two- and three-car garages, block-wall backyards and desert or low-water landscaping. Single-story floor plans are everywhere, though two-story homes are common in the newer all-ages subdivisions.

  • Original townsite: smaller, older homes on the blocks south of Bell Road, where the city began.
  • Active adult golf communities: single-level homes from the late 1990s and 2000s, often on or near a fairway.
  • All-ages master-planned communities: 2000s-era tract homes plus newer construction in areas such as Marley Park and Asante, where builders are still active.
  • Townhomes and condos: available, though detached homes make up most of what you will see on the market.

Because so much of the city is relatively new, buyers often compare resale homes against brand-new builder inventory a few miles away. Teigh can help you weigh both.

Sun City Grand (The Grand)

Del Webb developed Sun City Grand from 1996 to 2005, and the community now goes by The Grand. It is an age-restricted active adult community with four golf courses (Cimarron, Desert Springs, Granite Falls North and Granite Falls South), a Village Center, fitness and spa buildings, pools, and tennis, pickleball and bocce courts. Ask for the association's current occupancy rules before you write an offer.

Marley Park

Marley Park is a master-planned community in the 85379 ZIP code, roughly near Bell and Litchfield roads. Amenities include a community pool, clubhouse, fitness room, fire pits, playgrounds, parks and walking paths. Builders have continued adding new neighborhoods here in recent years.

Surprise Farms

Surprise Farms is a large master association made up of several sub-associations, with homes largely built in the early to mid-2000s. Some neighborhoods have a clubhouse, community pool, tennis courts, green spaces and play areas. Because it is split into sub-associations, two homes a few streets apart can have different HOA rules and dues.

Asante

Asante is a newer community near Loop 303 in northwest Surprise, with Lennar among the builders. Amenities include a clubhouse, pool, basketball and pickleball courts, and a playground, and White Tank Mountain Regional Park is close by.

Surprise has a lot of choice, which makes the homework more important. Here is what Teigh walks buyers through before an offer goes in:

  • HOA rules and fees. Nearly every subdivision has an HOA, and many have a master association plus a sub-association. Ask for the CC&Rs, the current dues, any transfer or capital fees charged at closing, and the rules on parking, RVs, rentals and exterior paint.
  • Solar panels. Many Surprise roofs carry solar. Find out whether the system is owned outright, financed, or leased. A lease usually has to be transferred to the buyer, and the solar company has its own approval process.
  • Pools. A pool is a big plus in July, but have it inspected separately. Ask about the pump, the age of the plaster and any barrier fencing.
  • Water and utilities. Depending on the address, water may come from the City of Surprise or from a private provider such as EPCOR, and electric service may be APS or SRP. Confirm the providers for any specific home.
  • Age rules. If a home is inside an age-restricted community, read the occupancy rules carefully before you commit.

Teigh's buyer services cover lender referrals, tours, offers and inspections, all the way to closing.

Surprise buyers usually have options, so a listing has to answer their questions quickly. The ones that come up most often are: How old is the roof? Is the solar owned or leased? What are the HOA dues and what do they cover? How old are the AC units and water heater? Is the pool equipment in good shape?

Having those answers ready, along with clean, bright rooms in the listing photos, helps a home compete with nearby new construction. Teigh includes staging help for her listing clients, from a room-by-room plan to full staging with her own furniture. You can see how that works on the home staging page.

Pricing in Surprise varies a lot by community, lot, view and upgrades, so Teigh prepares a comparative market analysis (CMA) for each home instead of relying on citywide averages. She never promises a price or a timeline. She does promise to explain every step.

Loop 303 runs north-south along the western side of the city and connects south to I-10 and northeast to I-17. US-60, known locally as Grand Avenue, cuts diagonally through Surprise toward Phoenix. Bell Road crosses the city east to west, meets Loop 303 at an interchange, and continues east to Loop 101 at the Peoria-Glendale line.

Valley Metro runs an express bus between Surprise and Glendale. Most residents drive, so think about your regular routes when you compare neighborhoods: a home near Loop 303 and a home near Grand Avenue can mean very different commutes.

Dysart Unified School District serves most of Surprise, and Nadaburg Unified School District serves a small section in the north. Ottawa University opened a campus in the city in 2017. Always check the assigned schools for a specific address with the district, since boundaries can change.

The city maintains more than a dozen parks. Shopping and dining cluster along Bell Road, around the Recreation Campus and in the Prasada area near Loop 303.

Teigh Wade is a REALTOR® with HomeSmart Elite Group, HomeSmart, and she was born in Phoenix and has spent most of her life in the West Valley. Her mission, in her words: "“Getting The Sale” is NOT my mission. Helping people navigate through every process of Real Estate is."

Teigh also offers mobile buyer and listing consultations, so she can meet you at your current home or at a coffee shop near the Recreation Campus. Because she is based right here, her mobile notary service reaches Surprise homes, offices and care facilities on short notice too. Call or text 480-550-2871.

faqs.q: Is Surprise, AZ an incorporated city?
faqs.a: Yes. Surprise incorporated as a city in 1960 and sits in Maricopa County in the northwest part of the Phoenix area. Flora Mae Statler founded the original townsite in 1938. Some nearby addresses, such as Waddell and the unincorporated Sun City communities, are not part of the city, so check the jurisdiction for any home you are considering.

Loop 303 and US-60 (Grand Avenue) are the main highways. Loop 303 runs along the west side of the city and links to I-10 to the south and I-17 to the northeast. Grand Avenue runs diagonally toward Phoenix, and Bell Road connects east to Loop 101 at the Peoria-Glendale line.

faqs.q: Do most homes in Surprise have an HOA?
faqs.a: Most do. The majority of Surprise homes are inside master-planned communities, and many have both a master association and a sub-association. Dues, transfer fees and rules vary widely, so Teigh requests the HOA documents early and goes over parking, rental and exterior rules with buyers before the inspection period ends.

Yes. Sun City Grand, now known as The Grand, is an age-restricted active adult community that Del Webb built between 1996 and 2005. Occupancy rules are set by the community's governing documents and federal housing law, so review the current requirements with the association before you buy. Teigh's guide to buying in a 55+ community covers the basics.

faqs.q: Where is spring training in Surprise?
faqs.a: Surprise Stadium, on the Surprise Recreation Campus near Bell Road and Bullard Avenue, is the spring training home of the Texas Rangers and the Kansas City Royals. The same campus includes Surprise Community Park, a fishing lake, a tennis and racquet complex, and the Oasis Swim center.

Dysart Unified School District serves most of Surprise, and Nadaburg Unified School District serves a small northern section. School assignments depend on the exact address and can change, so confirm boundaries directly with the district for any home you are considering before you make a decision.

faqs.q: What should I ask about solar on a Surprise home?
faqs.a: Ask whether the solar system is owned, financed or leased. An owned system usually transfers with the home. A financed or leased system often requires the buyer to take over a contract, and the solar company has its own approval steps and paperwork. Get the agreement early so your lender and you can review it.

faqs.q: How much is my Surprise home worth?
faqs.a: Values vary by community, lot, view, condition and upgrades, so there is no single answer for the city. Teigh prepares a comparative market analysis (CMA) based on recent nearby sales and current competition. Request one on the home value page or call or text 480-550-2871 for a no-obligation consultation.
